reason: The sources provide sufficient details for a compelling true story supported by multiple citations.
story: For centuries, historians believed that the wealthy Roman resort town of Herculaneum escaped the AD 79 eruption of Mount Vesuvius entirely. Because early excavations revealed almost no human remains, scholars assumed every inhabitant had successfully fled. That comforting narrative shattered in the 1980s when archaeologists excavated the ancient shoreline and found hundreds of skeletons huddled inside the vaulted stone boat houses. Trapped by the rising tide and blocked by the raging sea, about 300 desperate residents had waited for rescue boats that never arrived. At around 1 am on August 25, a superheated pyroclastic surge rushed down the mountain at 100 mph, plunging into the town with temperatures exceeding 900 degrees Fahrenheit. The intense thermal shock caused instant death, vaporizing soft tissue and leaving behind families frozen in their final moments, forever altering our understanding of history's most infamous volcanic disaster.
angle: For nearly 2,000 years, historians believed everyone in Herculaneum escaped Vesuvius—until excavators opened the shoreline boat houses and found 300 skeletons trapped inside.

claims.claim: Herculaneum was buried under volcanic material during the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in 79 AD.

evidence.quote: Herculaneum was buried under a massive pyroclastic flow in the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in 79 AD.
Both cities were destroyed by the A.D. 79 eruption of Vesuvius.

claims.claim: For centuries, scholars believed that the population of Herculaneum had time to escape the eruption.

evidence.quote: Archaeologists have long held that almost all Herculaneum's population had time to escape Vesuvius's wrath.
It was once believed the people of Herculaneum escaped Vesuvius’s 79AD eruption because of the lack of human remains discovered in the town.

claims.claim: Victims huddled in the vaulted stone chambers or fornici along the ancient beachfront hoping to escape by sea.

evidence.quote: It also appears that they were the last refuge for many of the people of Herculaneum.
These seaside boatsheds, about 10 meters long, became the final refuge for around 300 people who hoped to escape the eruption by sea.

claims.claim: The inhabitants who sheltered in the boat houses died instantly from extreme thermal shock rather than ash suffocation.

evidence.quote: Multidisciplinary research on the lethal effects of the pyroclastic surges in the Vesuvius area has shown that, in the vicinity of Pompeii and Herculaneum, intense heat was the main cause of the death of people who had previously been thought to have died by ash suffocation.
Death came instantly. Superheated gas from the pyroclastic surge reached temperatures above 900°F, causing immediate thermal shock.

claims.claim: The city of Herculaneum was rediscovered by chance in 1709 during the drilling of a well.

evidence.quote: According to the traditional tale, the city was rediscovered by chance in 1709 during the drilling of a well.
All traces of Pompeii and Herculaneum had been lost until 1709, when a well digger accidentally struck the stage.

claims.claim: Pliny the Younger documented the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in surviving letters written to the Roman historian Tacitus.

evidence.quote: The course and timeline of the eruption can be reconstructed based on archaeological excavations and two letters from Pliny the Younger to the Roman historian Tacitus.

The history of Vesuvius really begins with that description. Only one other account of the cataclysm at Vesuvius has survived the Dark Ages. Indeed, if Pliny's letters had perished, no one in the 18th century would have known that they were unearthing Herculaneum and later Pompeii.

claims.claim: Advanced X-ray techniques and AI helped researchers reveal text on carbonized papyrus scrolls that were previously unreadable.

evidence.quote: In 2024 the winners of a contest called the Vesuvius Challenge, with the help of AI, managed to reveal hundreds of words across 15 columns of text, corresponding to around 5% of a scroll.
The researchers, headed by physicist Vito Mocella, applied a state-of-the-art method, X-ray phase-contrast tomography, to examine the writing without harming the papyrus.

disputed: The exact month of the eruption is debated; traditional accounts point to August 24, but autumn indicators like heavy clothing, fresh produce, and sealed wine jars suggest October or November. The script should attribute autumn details to recent archaeological findings.
